2. Facts of the case, in brief am as follows: The opposite party No. 1 here as plaintiff filed Title suit No. 197 of 1977 in the 4th Court of the Subordinate Judge Dacca for a declaration that the decree dated 20.9.1972 passed in Title suit No. 35 of 1971 of the 3rd Court of the Subordinate Judge, Dacca in respect of the suit property was void, illegal and not binding upon the plaintiff and also for a declaration that the Kabala obtained through court in execution of the decree of the aforesaid title suit was null and void. The case of the plaintiff was that the suit property along with other properties belonged to 3 brothers Nibaran Chandra Mitra, Abinash Chandra Mitre and Satish Chandra Mitre by purchase. On an amicable partition among the brothers, Abinash Chandra got the suit property and died thereafter leaving behind three sons Santi Priya, Chitta Priya and Snehamoy the present opposite parties 3 to 5 as heirs. The opposite parties 3 to 5 transferred the suit property to plaintiff by a deed of exchange registered on 30.5.63 through their attorney Syed Amir Ali. Opposite party No. 1 filed Title suit No. 35 of 1971 in the 3rd Court of the Subordinate Judge, Dacca against opposite parties 3 to 6 for specific performance of contract in respect of the suit property and got an ex party decree and thereafter by putting the decree in execution got a kabala executed through court. The plaintiff thereafter filed Title suit No. 197 of 1977 for declaration as aforesaid on the allegation that the defendant No. 12 had obtained the decree by fraudulent suppression of processes and has thereafter obtained a kabala through court in execution by practicing fraud upon the court. 

 3. The suit was contested by the petitioners here who were defendants 2 and 3 in this suit. The defendant No. 2 claimed to purchase from defendant No. 1. Defendant No. 3 is the husband of defeating No. 2. The suit was contested by denying all material allegations of the plaint. The case of the defence was in short that the plaintiff had no title to the suit property as claimed by her and no locus standi to file the suit. It was contended that the deed of exchange on the strength of which the plaintiff claimed title in the suit property was fraudulent and without consideration. It was averred that processes were duly served and they were not suppressed and the ex party decree was obtained in due course of law and the kabala was executed and registered though court in accordance with the law. 

 6. The main grievance of Mr. Haider, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, is that the learned Appellate court as also the learned trial court have failed to give decisions on two issues relating to the title of the plaintiffs in the suit land and her locus standi though evidence was adduced in relation to these issues and that the courts below hay not considered material evidences produced by the defendants in support of their case relating to those issues. He has made other grievances also but in view of the order that we propose to make in the case we do not consider it necessary to state those grievances. 

 "(a) Has the plaintiff her claimed title to the suit property ? 

 (b) Has the plaintiff locaus standi to file the suit" ? 

 9. Confronted with this situation, Mr. B. N. Chowdhury the learned Advocate for the opposite parties has contended that though the learned trial court and the learned appellate court did not take up these issues specifically for decision, they have in fact, decided these issues. We have gone through the judgment of the learned trial court and it appears that he has observed that in the present suit as it has been framed there is no scope for going to the matter relating to the question of title. "We have not been able to appreciate the logic of the trial court when an issue on title had specifically been framed. There was also no scope for the learned Additional District Judge to avoid giving a decision in the matter which he appears to have done. The learned Additional District Judge has observed that in the suit, he was required to see whether the plaintiff had locus-standi to file the suit and by referring practically only to the documents of exchange, he came to the conclusion that the plaintiff had locus-standi. He did not consider the case of the defence that the plaintiff had no properties in Murshidabad with which the properties of the Mitras in Bangladesh were alleged to have been exchanged and the evidence filed on the side of the defence in support of their contention that the plaintiff had no properties at Murshidabad. He has only gone into the matter superficially. This was a suit for declaration that a decree passed against some third parties in a suit in which the plaintiff was not a party was void and without jurisdiction and the locus stated on which the plaintiff relied was that she owned the properties by exchange. Before the plaintiff can he given a declaration under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act she had to prove before the court that she had the legal character or the right to property she claimed and unless the plaintiff could prove such legal character or right to property, she could not be given any declaratory relief. In view of the provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, we are of the opinion that since the plaintiff’s entitlement to maintain the suit was based on the ownership of the property she claimed, the question of title of the plaintiff was directly and substantially in issue in the suit and without deciding this issue the plaintiff could not have been given any relief under section 43 of the Specific Relief Act which she prayed for. A decision on the issue of title would also decide her locus steal to file the suit. In the circumstances, the trial court has committed an error of law apparent on the face of the record not only in not incorporating these additional issues framed at the instance of the defendants specifically in the judgment and stating his decision thereon but also in holding that in the suit before him there was no scope to go deep into the matter. It is true that the finding of the trial court that the suit was maintainable without a prayer for declaration of title cannot be found fault with but that does not mean that in a suit of the present nature the question of title cannot be gone into deep and that even on the face of specific issues framed in the suit. It also appears from the appellate judgment that the learned appellate court was of the view that it was not a suit for declaration of title and it was enough if the plaintiff has been able to make out a prima facie case that he has right, title and interest in the disputed property, we find no basis for the proposition that in a suit of the present nature, it was enough if the plaintiff could make out a prima facie case that he has right, title and interest in the suit property. The learned appellate court failed to consider that the learned trial court has failed to state his findings and decision on the additional issues framed and has failed to consider the defence case and the evidence adduced before the trial court as also the additional evidence adduced before him to substantiate the defence case that the deed of exchange was fraudulent and without consideration. We refrain from making any comment on the worth of the evidence that were adduced by the parties in support of the title claimed by the plaintiff or in negativing the title of the plaintiff lest this should prejudice the rehearing which we propose to order in this case. Mr. Chowdhury has contended that the learned appellate court has found that the plaintiff has title in the suit property. We have already observed that the learned appellate Court merely concerned itself in finding a prima facie title and on the face of what the learned appellate court has itself observed on the judgment. Mr. Chowdhury cannot be heard to say that the learned Appellate Court has found title in plaintiff. Mr. Chowdhury could not place before as any decision to prove his alternative contention that a prima facie title in a suit of this nature was, enough. 

 10. Mr. Chowdhury, has, however, taken up an alternative line of argument. He has contended that when an order is obtained from the court by practicing fraud upon the court the Court has inherent power to vacate that order mom. He has relief upon the case laws reported in 20 DLR (Dacca) 937 (Abel Kalam Rahmatallah vs. Md. Ashique) and A.LR. 1948 Nagpur 52 (Ballabhdas Lachminarayan Mahethwari vs. Sobhaji Kesharesingh and another.) Both these cases relate to the question of the inherent power of the court to set aside a sale held in an execution proceeding on the ground of fraud practiced upon the court. In 20 D.L.R. case, it was held that where auction sale has been procured by practicing fraud on court, the executing court in case like this does not become functus officio even where the auction sale has been confirmed, sale certificate issued and possession delivered, but under its inherent powers under section 151 Court is competent to set aside the sale. The decision of the Nagpur case is also to similar effect. It was held that the practice of fraud on the court is a serious matter and it renders void everything which is founded on such fraud. It is not only within the powers but it is the duty of the court to take notice of such fraud when detected or brought to its notice. The court cannot permit a party guilty of a fraud on the court to enjoy what it has secured thereby. The facts of the two reported decisions are however, of somewhat exceptional nature with which the facts of the present case has no semblance. Besides in the 20 D.L.R. case the court had held that the court had not become focus officio. But so far as the case before as is concerned, we are of the opinion that once the court has passed an ex parte decree, it becomes functus officio and it is beyond the powers of the court to exercise its inherent jurisdiction to set aside the decree on detecting fraud. In such case, the remedy of an aggrieved person lies in the specific provisions of the C.P.C. as, for example, in filing an application under Order 9, rule 13 C.P.C. or an appeal or in a separate suit for setting aside the decree on grounds of fraud, as has in fact been done in this case. The inherent powers of the court. cannot be invoked. We are of the firm opinion that so far as the ex parte decree is concerned the court has no power to vacate it and set it aside even on detection of fraud at a subsequent stage. The next question is whether the order passed in the execution case alleged to be obtained fraudulently is liable to be declared void. Mr. Chowdhury has contended that as required by P.O. 142 of 1972, an affidavit was filed by an officer of the court on the basis of an affidavit filed by defendant No. 1 Wares Ali and Wares An had sworn a false affidavit to the effect that the Mitras were Bangladeshi nationals though it was evident that they are Indian nationals. What has happened in this case is that on the basis of an affidavit which is alleged to be false, the court, it is stated, has directed its officer to swear an affidavit before the Registrar and on the basis of that the Registrar has registered the document. The case has, therefore, traveled far beyond the hands of the Court and the court has no longer any seisin over the matter. If any fraud has been practiced, it has been practiced in the matter of registration and the court obviously exercises no inherent power to set aside and vacate the registration done by the Registrar. Besides, even for getting a declaration that the registration was null and void for contravention of the provision of P.O. 142 of 1972, a party seeking the declaration must prove his legal character or right to property and if this has not been proved, he cannot get a declaration under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. In this view of the matter, even for getting a declaration that the transfer was null and void being hit by the provisions of P.O. 142 of 1972, the plaintiff has to prove her legal character or right to property. The contention of the learned Advocate that the ex parte decree and the sale-document having been brought about by practicing fraud on the court, the court has inherent jurisdiction to set aside the decree as well as the sale is not, therefore, tenable. Forbearance by the courts below to decide issues framed compels us to remand the suit for a rehearing and we are of the opinion that the case should be remanded to the trial court for a rehearing of the suit and for stating its findings and decisions on all issues including the two additional issues framed at the instance of the defendants on 15.6.77.
